title: Probing chaos and thermalization through out-of-time-ordered correlators in random field spin chains
authors: C Jisha, Shivam Mishra, Ravi Prakash
abstract: Out-of-time-ordered correlators (OTOCs) have emerged as a diagnostic of information scrambling and quantum chaos in many-body systems. We investigate the imprints of chaos in the dynamics of OTOCs in the Heisenberg spin-$1/2$ chain with random fields. The system is parameterized to exhibit a crossover from integrable to chaotic dynamics. We demonstrate numerically that the approach to saturation of the OTOC can distinguish between integrable and chaotic regimes, with a power-law $(1/t)$ relaxation for integrable systems and a higher-degree power-law decay $(1/t^α; α\ge 1)$ followed by an exponential relaxation for the chaotic regime. We further show that long-range spectral statistics, such as the number variance, are more effective in characterizing quantum chaos in the regime near saturation of OTOC. We also demonstrate that the relaxation and initial scrambling regimes exhibit distinct and universal features, with the former being sensitive and the latter being robust against different realizations of random-fields. The long-time saturation of OTOC also fluctuates with different realizations, and its exact expression is derived through the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis.
summary: The paper uses Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlators and spectral statistics to probe quantum chaos in a random field spin chain. It establishes that the decay dynamics of these correlators—specifically distinguishing between power-law and exponential relaxation—can precisely map out the transition from integrable to chaotic or localized phases as disorder increases.
main_problem: The study investigates how quantum chaos and thermalization manifest in many-body systems by analyzing Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlators (OTOCs). The goal is to distinguish between different dynamical regimes, such as integrable, chaotic, and Many-Body Localized (MBL) phases.
main_result: The OTOC dynamics provide a clear diagnostic tool: integrable systems show power-law $(1/t)$ relaxation, while chaotic systems exhibit higher-degree power-law decay followed by exponential relaxation. Spectral statistics like the number variance confirm these transitions across different disorder strengths.
method: The authors use theoretical diagnostics including OTOCs, Nearest Neighbor Spacing Distribution (NNSD), and Number Variance ($\Sigma_2(r)$) applied to a random field spin chain Hamiltonian. They analyze the time evolution of these quantities in different energy eigenbases.
model_or_system: The system is a Heisenberg spin-1/2 chain subjected to random fields, described by $H_{II} = H_I + \sum h_i\sigma_x^i + \sum g_i\sigma_z^i$. The disorder strength ($k$) acts as the primary tuning parameter controlling the transition between integrable, chaotic, and MBL regimes.
key_observables: Out-of-Time-Ordered Correlators (OTOCs), Number Variance ($\Sigma_2(r)$), Nearest Neighbor Spacing Distribution (NNSD), and Entanglement Entropy ($S_A$).
important_parameters: Disorder strength ($k$), time $t$, and the comparison between power-law decay vs. exponential decay rates.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on comparing numerical results to predictions from Random Matrix Theory (RMT) and utilizing the Eigenstate Thermalization Hypothesis (ETH) for long-time saturation values.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the crossover of NNSD from Poisson to Wigner statistics with increasing disorder, plot $\Sigma_2(r)$ showing transitions between linear and GOE behavior, and track OTOC decay rates distinguishing power-law vs. exponential relaxation.
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes the dynamics across three time regimes (scrambling, relaxation, saturation) using multiple diagnostics (OTOCs, spectral statistics). It maps out a phase diagram based on disorder strength ($k$), confirming transitions between integrable, chaotic, and MBL phases.
why_interesting: This work provides quantitative signatures for quantum chaos in disordered many-body systems, offering robust theoretical tools (like OTOC analysis) to distinguish fundamental dynamical regimes relevant to non-equilibrium physics.
